title: used to and would for past habits
tagline: How things were, again and again, before they changed — but only one form works for states.
why: Reading Part 6's open cloze regularly tests used to/didn't use to as a missing grammar word, and Speaking Part 4 asks you to compare life now with life before — the natural home of used to and would. Knowing that would can't describe a state (like be, have or like) is the single detail that separates a confident B1 answer from a shaky one.

hook.text: Miss Vega: “When I was a new teacher here, we didn't use to have computers in class!” Mateo: “Did you use to write everything on the board?” Miss Vega: “Yes — and we'd often lose the chalk!”
hook.ask: Miss Vega uses three past-habit forms in bold. Which ones can also describe a state (like not having computers), and which one is only for repeated actions?

use.point: used to for past habits that are different now

examples.note: a repeated habit, not true anymore

examples.text: Miss Vega used to teach in a much smaller classroom.
Did you use to walk to school, Miss Vega?
examples.note: the question form: did + use to

use.point: used to for past states (be, have, like)

examples.note: a state, not an action — used to can describe this

examples.text: We didn't use to have computers in every classroom.
examples.note: negative state — didn't use to + have

use.point: would for repeated past actions (not states)

examples.text: Miss Vega'd always bring extra chalk to class.
The students would often share one textbook between three people.
On Fridays, the whole school would gather outside for assembly.
examples.note: a habitual event, repeated every week

use.point: would can't describe states, and used to vs be used to

examples.text: We used to have only one computer — you can't say would have here.
examples.note: would doesn't work with states like have, be, like

examples.text: At first the new building felt strange, but now everyone is used to it.
examples.note: be used to = familiar with something now, a different idea altogether

watch_out.wrong: The school would be much smaller.
watch_out.right: The school used to be much smaller.
watch_out.why: Would can't describe a state like be — only used to works here.

watch_out.wrong: We use to have three classrooms.
watch_out.why: Used to always ends in -d, even though it sounds like use to in speech.

watch_out.wrong: Did you used to walk to school?
watch_out.why: After did, the verb goes back to its base form: use to, not used to.

watch_out.wrong: Miss Vega used to like walking to school every Friday, again and again.
watch_out.right: Miss Vega would walk to school every Friday.
watch_out.why: For a clearly repeated action (not a state), would sounds more natural once used to has already set the scene.

watch_out.wrong: I am used to walk to school now.
watch_out.right: I'm used to walking to school now.
watch_out.why: Be used to is followed by -ing (or a noun), not the infinitive — it means 'familiar with', a different meaning from used to.

watch_out.wrong: We didn't used to have computers.
watch_out.why: The negative uses didn't + use to (base form), never didn't used to.

l1.why: Solía + infinitivo needs the full form used to + infinitive in English, not just used.

l1.es: El colegio antes era más pequeño.
l1.wrong: The school was smaller before, all the time.
l1.why: Spanish antes + imperfecto for a changed state becomes used to + be in English.

l1.es: Solíamos compartir un libro entre tres.
l1.wrong: We would share one book between three, that was normal.
l1.right: We used to share one book between three.
l1.why: For a general past habit (not clearly repeated events), used to is the safer, more natural choice than would.

l1.es: Ya me he acostumbrado a las clases nuevas.
l1.wrong: I used to the new classes now.
l1.right: I'm used to the new classes now.
l1.why: Acostumbrarse a = be used to (familiar with now), completely different from the past-habit used to.

remember.trick: USED TO for how it WAS — not anymore!
remember.tip: If you can replace it with a state verb like be, have or like, only used to works — would is for repeated actions only.

dialogue.title: How the school used to be
dialogue.context: For the school's anniversary, Mateo, Sofia, Liam and Nadia interview Miss Vega about what school life used to be like.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Miss Vega, what did the school use to be like?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: It used to be much smaller — just two buildings!

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Did you use to have computers in class?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: No, we didn't use to have any — we wrote everything on the board.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: And we'd often lose the chalk, right?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Every week! Students would always “borrow” it for something else.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Did you use to walk to school like us?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Yes, and on Fridays the whole school would gather outside for assembly.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: It sounds so different from now.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: It was! But I'm used to the new building already — I love it.

can_do: I can talk about past habits and states that are different now with used to.
I can use would for actions that happened again and again in the past.
I can ask and answer questions with did you use to…? and understand be used to as a different idea.
summary: Used to + infinitive = a past habit or state that isn't true anymore.
Would + infinitive = a repeated past action, but never a state like be, have or like.
The negative and question forms are didn't use to / Did you use to…? — never used to in these two.
Used to is the safer choice for a general past situation; would works best once the scene is already set.
Be used to (+ -ing) means familiar with something now — a completely different idea from the past habit used to.
